By Maurie Backman Published November 1, 2026, 4:33pm ET · 3 min read 𝕏 f ⧉ Quick Read Social Security's trust fund may run dry by 2032, triggering a 22% benefit cut affecting all recipients nationwide. New Jersey retirees face the steepest impact, losing roughly $503 monthly ($6,040 yearly) on the state's average $2,288 benefit. Retirees should offset potential cuts through part-time work, spending reductions, or relocating to a more affordable state. © gguy44 There’s a lot to love about living in New Jersey — and a lot not to like. New Jersey has some of the highest property and income taxes in the country. For workers who earn large wages, those costs may be manageable. But for retirees on Social Security, the Garden State can be a tough place to call home. Making matters worse is that Social Security recipients in New Jersey could soon see their benefits shrink by more than $6,000 a year. Here’s why, and how seniors can plan. Social Security cuts may be coming for everyone It’s not just New Jersey seniors who may see their Social Security benefits reduced. The program is looking at potentially implementing sweeping cuts as early as 2032. The reason is that the program’s trust fund is expected to run dry at that point, and Social Security won’t be able to cover its costs on incoming payroll tax revenue alone. If Congress can’t find a way to shore up Social Security’s finances, cuts may be inevitable. The Social Security Trustees project a possible 22% cut once there’s no more trust fund to tap. That percentage could still wiggle based on how much revenue Social Security receives in the coming years, though. Meanwhile, the average Social Security benefit in New Jersey is $2,288 per month. If there’s a 22% cut, the typical recipient could lose out on $503 per month, or about $6,040 per year. As it is, many seniors struggle to stay in the Garden State due to the high cost. If Social Security is actually cut, more older residents could end up fleeing the state. Now on the one hand, that might open up the housing market for younger buyers who want proximity to major cities like New York City and Philadelphia. But it could also force many seniors into a tough decision. How to plan for Social Security cuts Social Security cuts are not guaranteed to happen. Congress has never allowed Social Security to cut benefits before, and there are different reforms that can be implemented to prevent a reduction this time around. But it’s best to plan for Social Security cuts, no matter where you live. And part of that could mean having an income plan to make up for the lost money. What you should do is take a look at your monthly Social Security check and figure out what a 22% cut might amount to. Then, explore options for compensating. Let’s say a 22% cut would reduce your Social Security payments by $500 a month. If you can work part-time and earn the $500, you should be set. If that’s not doable but you’re able to trim $500 in spending from your budget, that works as well. And if you’re a retiree in New Jersey who’s struggling on Social Security, you may want to consider relocating to a part of the country where costs are more affordable, especially if you intend to keep owning a home. You can always come back to your home town for a week at the shore. But you may find that your Social Security checks can go a lot further in another state.
